terms.meaning: A layer of gases, dust and water vapour around the Earth, about 1000 km thick.
Weather: conditions of a place at one time. Climate: the average over a long period.
Incoming solar radiation from the Sun to the Earth.
A line on a map joining places with the same temperature.
A line on a map joining places with the same pressure.
The calm belt with little wind at the equator. Also called the ITCZ.
The amount of water vapour in the air. A hygrometer measures it.
The leeward side of a mountain, which gets little rain. Hassan is one, while Mangaluru is windward.

items.name: Gases in the air
items.formula: Nitrogen 78.08%, Oxygen 20.94%.
items.example: The remaining 1% is mostly Argon (0.93%), with Carbon dioxide (0.03%).

items.name: Troposphere
items.formula: Lowest layer: up to 18 km at the equator and 8 km at the poles.
items.example: All weather happens here.

items.name: Stratosphere
items.formula: Up to 50 km. Ozone here absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet rays.
items.example: No clouds, so it is ideal for jet aircraft.

items.name: Mesosphere
items.formula: Up to 80 km, and the coldest layer.
items.example: Temperature falls as you go up.

items.name: Thermosphere and Exosphere
items.formula: Thermosphere (Ionosphere): very hot, and its ions reflect radio waves. Exosphere: top layer, very thin.
items.example: The five layers from the ground: Tropo, Strato, Meso, Thermo, Exo.

items.name: Normal lapse rate
items.formula: Temperature falls about 6.4°C for each 1 km of height.
items.example: Climbing 3 km, it falls about 19.2°C.

items.name: Inversion of temperature
items.formula: Temperature rises with height in some cases.
items.example: Mountain valleys on long, clear, still winter nights over snow.

items.name: Temperature zones
items.formula: Torrid: 0° to 23°30'. Temperate: 23°30' to 66°30'. Frigid: 66°30' to 90°.
items.example: Both north and south of the equator.

items.name: Hottest and coldest places
items.formula: Hottest: Al Aziziya, Libya. Coldest: Vostok, Antarctica.
items.example: In India: Ganganagar in Rajasthan and Leh in Ladakh.

items.name: Atmospheric pressure
items.formula: Measured by a barometer in millibars; 1013.25 mb at sea level.
items.example: It drops about 34 mb per 300 metres, and higher temperature gives lower pressure.

items.name: Seven pressure belts
items.formula: Equatorial low (0-5°), Sub-tropical high (30-35°), Sub-polar low (60-65°), Polar high (80-90°).
items.example: All but the equatorial one come in a north and a south pair, giving 7.

items.name: Wind instruments
items.formula: Wind vane: direction. Anemometer: speed.
items.example: Wind is the horizontal movement of air.

items.name: Planetary winds
items.formula: Trade: sub-tropical high to equator. Westerlies: sub-tropical high to sub-polar low. Polar: polar high to sub-polar low.
items.example: Strong southern westerlies: Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Shrieking Sixties.

items.name: India's monsoon winds
items.formula: South-west: June to September. North-east: late September to mid-December.
items.example: These are seasonal winds.

items.name: Local wind names
items.formula: Loo (India), Chinook (USA), Fohn (Alps), Mistral (France), Sirocco (Sahara).
items.example: Also Brick Fielder (Australia) and Blizzard (Antarctica).

items.name: Cyclone and anti-cyclone
items.formula: Cyclone: low at the centre, winds spiral in, anti-clockwise in the north. Anti-cyclone: high at the centre, winds blow out, clockwise in the north.
items.example: Typhoon (Japan, China), Hurricane (USA, Mexico), Willy willies (Australia).

items.name: Relative humidity
items.formula: Actual water vapour ÷ the most the air can hold × 100.
items.example: If air holds 10 g and could hold 20 g, RH = 50%.

items.name: Four cloud types
items.formula: Stratus: low sheets, fair weather. Cumulus: cauliflower, rain. Cirrus: highest, feathery, fair. Nimbus: dark, heavy rain.
items.example: Cirrus is called mare's tail; cumulus is called wool packs.

items.name: Three types of rainfall
items.formula: Convectional: heated air rises ("afternoon rain"). Orographic: a mountain forces air up. Cyclonic: air rises in a cyclone.
items.example: Mangaluru gets orographic rain.

items.name: Rainfall records
items.formula: Wettest: Mawsynram, 1140 cm a year. Driest: Atacama, Chile.
items.example: Agumbe is the Cherrapunji of South India; Royli gets just 8.3 cm.

mistakes.text: Ozone is in the stratosphere, but weather changes happen in the troposphere below it.
High temperature means low pressure, because warm air expands. The two are inversely related.
Cyclones turn anti-clockwise in the north and clockwise in the south. Anti-cyclones do the reverse.
Meteorology studies weather, and Climatology studies climate.
